reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Von Noorden's Binocular Vision and Ocular Motility
clinicalPearls: Characterised by a small central suppression scotoma in the deviating eye with intact peripheral fusion, giving gross but subnormal stereopsis
The manifest deviation (microtropia) is typically small, often 8 prism dioptres or less, and can be easy to miss on cover testing
Frequently represents the best achievable sensory outcome after surgical alignment of infantile esotropia
May arise primarily or secondary to anisometropia, a small unilateral macular lesion, or residual misalignment after strabismus surgery
The 4-prism-dioptre base-out test helps demonstrate the central scotoma by showing absence of a refixation movement in the affected eye
Worth four-dot testing shows fusion at near (peripheral field) but suppression at distance (central field)
Peripheral fusion preserves some motor fusion amplitude and binocular cooperation despite the central scotoma
Amblyopia is common in the non-fixating eye and should be actively sought and treated
reference.pathophysiology: Monofixation syndrome reflects a compromise in binocular sensory function in which a small central suppression scotoma develops in one eye to eliminate diplopia and confusion, while peripheral retinal correspondence and fusion are retained. This produces a stable small-angle deviation. Recognised triggers include anisometropia (unequal refraction), a small unilateral macular lesion, and residual misalignment after correction of a larger childhood strabismus. Because high-grade central stereopsis is lost but peripheral fusion persists, stereoacuity is reduced but not abolished, and the patient retains a degree of comfortable binocular vision.
additionalDifferentials: Orthotropia with normal binocular single vision
additionalInvestigations: Cover/uncover and alternate prism cover testing to detect and quantify the small deviation
4-prism-dioptre base-out test to demonstrate the central suppression scotoma
Worth four-dot test to distinguish peripheral fusion from central suppression
Stereoacuity testing (e.g. Titmus or TNO) showing gross but subnormal stereopsis
Best-corrected visual acuity in each eye to detect amblyopia
Cycloplegic refraction to identify underlying anisometropia
redFlags: New-onset or increasing deviation suggesting decompensation
Dense amblyopia threatening visual development in a child
An unexplained macular lesion found on examination requiring further assessment
Diplopia developing where none was present, indicating loss of suppression
reference.prognosis: Monofixation syndrome is a stable and often favourable sensory state that provides peripheral fusion and gross stereopsis; many patients remain comfortably aligned long term, although associated amblyopia needs monitoring and the small deviation may occasionally decompensate.
pitfalls: Overlooking the small deviation on standard cover testing and labelling the patient orthotropic
Missing coexisting amblyopia in the non-fixating eye
Attempting to eliminate the small residual angle surgically and inducing intractable diplopia
Failing to correct anisometropia that underlies the condition
references: Von Noorden's Binocular Vision and Ocular Motility
management: Optical correction of any underlying anisometropia with spectacles or contact lenses
Treat associated amblyopia with occlusion or penalisation and monitor visual acuity
Reassure that the microtropia is a stable and often favourable sensory state providing peripheral fusion and gross stereopsis, so many patients need no intervention beyond refraction
Reserve prism correction or strabismus surgery for the minority in whom the small deviation decompensates into a symptomatic larger-angle strabismus
Periodic orthoptic monitoring of the deviation and stereoacuity to detect decompensation or worsening amblyopia
